resources.string: Glossary
From rows and hand ranks to scoops and best play
Row (front, middle, back)
The three groups your 13 cards are split into: 3 cards in the front, 5 in the middle, and 5 in the back. When everyone reveals, each row is compared with every opponent\'s matching row.
Hand rank

The category of a row, from highest to lowest: straight flush, quads (four of a kind), full house (trips plus a pair), flush, straight, trips, two pair, pair, high card. A higher category always wins; within the same category, higher cards win (A highest, 2 lowest; suits never rank). The front has only 3 cards, so it can only be trips, a pair, or high card.
A straight with A counted as 1. Rules vary by table: it can be the lowest straight, the second-highest straight, or not a straight at all. Set this in Settings › Rules.
Foul
The back must be at least as strong as the middle, and the middle at least as strong as the front. Any other order is a foul, which cannot be played.
Strict rows
A rule where equal rows (same category and ranks) also count as a foul: each row must be strictly stronger than the one in front of it.
Scoop
Winning all three rows against the same opponent, earning extra points depending on the rules. Losing all three rows to an opponent means being scooped.
Home run
Scooping all three opponents in a single hand, earning additional bonus points from each.
Front trips
Three of a kind in the front row. Because the front has only 3 cards, trips is its strongest possible hand, and many rules award extra points for it.
Special rows

Strong row hands that award bonus points: front trips, middle full house, quads or straight flush, and back quads or straight flush. Depending on the rules, every opponent pays regardless of who wins the row, or only opponents whose row you beat.
Dragon
Holding all 13 ranks from 2 through A. As long as you do not foul, every opponent pays you bonus points according to the rules.
Neural network

The model used for computer players and analysis: given a hand and an arrangement, it estimates the average score that arrangement earns. It was trained by playing a large number of hands against itself.
Q (expected points)
The average score an arrangement is expected to earn, estimated by the neural network against three opponents playing like it. Positive means winning points on average; negative means losing.
Best one
The arrangement with the highest Q—what the AI considers the best play. Arrangements very close to it (within the neural network\'s margin of error) are just as good.
Attacking / defending
The style of the best arrangement. Attacking: concentrates strength in one row, scooping more but also getting scooped more. Defending: balances the rows, getting scooped less while scooping less.
Playing for rows
An arrangement that focuses on winning individual rows rather than chasing scoops. Most important under rules that score every row.
Independent rows
A simpler computer player that estimates each row\'s chance of winning on its own, without considering how the three rows interact.
Monte Carlo
A computer player that tests each arrangement against many random deals for the opponents (set by independent rows) and picks the one with the best average score.
